Chapter 1: Arriving in a City on Edge — The Dodds Step into Berlin
Imagine what it feels like to step off a train or plane into a city buzzing with energy, but humming with something you can’t quite name. That’s exactly what the Dodd family experienced in the summer of 1933, trading the familiar warmth of the American South for Berlin—a city alive and restless, caught in the grip of change.
The father, a quiet history professor who’d always found comfort among his books, was suddenly tapped to serve as the U.S. ambassador to Germany. It wasn’t a job he’d chased, or even expected. He wasn’t a polished diplomat, and honestly, he preferred straight talk over political games. He brought his wife and two grown kids—a son and a daughter—along for the ride, each of them hopeful, but a little uncertain about what lay ahead.
At first glance, Berlin was a city of striking contrasts. The avenues were wide and busy, parks lush and green, and the cafés absolutely buzzing with conversation. But look just a little closer, and you’d spot swastika flags hanging from government buildings, and uniformed men—members of the new regime’s paramilitary squads—everywhere you turned. The city pulsed with excitement, but underneath it all, you could feel the tension, like a storm waiting to break.
The Dodds moved into a grand old house near the Tiergarten—that big, beautiful park right at Berlin’s heart. This place, once a symbol of American diplomacy, now seemed a bit faded, almost forgotten, much like America’s reputation in Germany at the time. The new ambassador? Well, he never quite got used to all the pomp. He liked to walk to work, think things through, and steer clear of the endless cocktail parties that so many diplomats seemed to love.
His daughter, though—she saw Berlin as one big adventure. Spirited and curious, she dove headfirst into the city’s dazzling nightlife. She went to parties, met artists, and mixed with both Germans and expats. For a moment, it felt like life might just go on as usual, despite the shadows creeping in.
But the truth was hard to avoid. Conversations turned careful, even among friends. People whispered about neighbors who had vanished or been arrested. The newspapers, once full of spirited debate, started echoing the government’s every word. Even the staff in the Dodds’ home grew more guarded—sometimes torn between loyalty to their jobs and allegiance to the new regime.
The ambassador, ever the historian, tried to fit the pieces together. He met officials, sat through ceremonies, and sent reports back to Washington, hoping, at first, that maybe this new government might steady a country battered by crisis. But with each passing month, it grew clear—Berlin was changing. And not for the better.
For the Dodd family, every day meant finding a balance: trying to understand this new world, hoping to build goodwill, but never quite able to shake the feeling that they were standing at the edge of something dangerous—something that might soon sweep across not just Berlin, but the whole world.
